description: Circular and hyperbolic trigonometry in both radians and degrees, angle conversion and unwrapping, the functions that build and decompose complex numbers, and the special and number-theoretic functions (gamma, beta, error functions, Bessel, Legendre, elliptic integrals, primes and combinatorics) that ship with core MATLAB.

tools.name: sin
tools.description: Computes the sine of each element, with the argument interpreted in radians. Use it to generate waveforms, to evaluate harmonic models and anywhere an angle is stored in radians. For complex input it returns the complex sine defined by the exponential formula.

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Angle in radians; numeric array, real or complex.

tools.notes: sin(pi) is about 1.22e-16 rather than exactly 0 because pi is not exactly representable. Use `sind` when your angles are in degrees so that sind(180) is exactly 0.

tools.name: cos
tools.description: Computes the cosine of each element in radians. It pairs with `sin` for quadrature signals, rotation matrices and Fourier series. Complex input is supported and follows the standard analytic continuation.
tools.example:
cos(0)
theta = pi/6;
R = [cos(theta) -sin(theta); sin(theta) cos(theta)]
R * [1; 0]
tools.notes: cos(pi/2) is about 6.1e-17, not 0. Use `cosd` for degree input when exactness at multiples of 90 matters.

tools.name: tan
tools.description: Computes the tangent of each element in radians. Because the tangent has poles at odd multiples of pi/2, expect very large values near those points rather than an error or Inf. Use it for slope calculations and in geometric transformations.
tools.example:
tan(pi/4)
tan(pi/2)
slope = tan(deg2rad(30))
tools.notes: tan(pi/2) returns about 1.6e16 rather than Inf because pi/2 is not exactly representable in binary floating point.

tools.name: asin
tools.description: Computes the inverse sine in radians, returning values in [-pi/2, pi/2] for real input in [-1, 1]. Arguments outside that range produce complex results rather than an error, which is a useful diagnostic that a normalization step went wrong. Use `asind` for a result in degrees.

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Numeric array; real values outside [-1,1] give complex output.

tools.example:
asin(1)
rad2deg(asin(0.5))
asin(1.5)
asind(0.5)
tools.notes: Floating-point rounding can push a computed cosine slightly above 1, which makes asin or acos return a complex value; clamp with `min(max(x,-1),1)` first.

tools.name: acos
tools.description: Computes the inverse cosine in radians, returning values in [0, pi] for real input in [-1, 1]. It is the standard way to recover an angle between two vectors from their normalized dot product. Values outside [-1, 1] return complex results.
tools.notes: For angles between vectors, `atan2(norm(cross(u,v)), dot(u,v))` is numerically better conditioned near 0 and pi than acos.

tools.name: atan
tools.description: Computes the inverse tangent in radians, returning values in (-pi/2, pi/2). Because it takes a single ratio it cannot distinguish quadrants, so use `atan2` when you have separate y and x components. Use `atand` for degrees.
tools.example:
rad2deg(atan(1))
atan(-1)
atan2(-1, -1)   % different quadrant
tools.notes: atan(y/x) loses the sign information of x, mapping the third quadrant onto the first; atan2 is almost always the correct choice for geometry.

tools.name: atan2
tools.description: Computes the four-quadrant inverse tangent of Y/X, returning an angle in (-pi, pi] that respects the signs of both arguments. Use it to convert Cartesian coordinates to a polar angle, to compute headings and to extract the phase of a complex number. It handles X = 0 correctly instead of dividing by zero.
tools.example:
rad2deg(atan2(1, 1))
rad2deg(atan2(1, -1))
rad2deg(atan2(-1, -1))
z = -1 + 1i;
isequal(atan2(imag(z), real(z)), angle(z))
tools.notes: `atan2d` returns degrees directly. For complex numbers `angle(z)` is equivalent and shorter. To get angles in [0, 2*pi) use `mod(atan2(y,x), 2*pi)`.

tools.name: sind
tools.description: Computes the sine with the argument given in degrees, returning exactly zero at multiples of 180 rather than a tiny rounding residue. Use it whenever your data is naturally in degrees, such as bearings, latitude and longitude, or mechanical angles. `cosd`, `tand`, `asind`, `acosd`, `atand` and `atan2d` complete the degree-based family.
tools.example:
sind(180)
sin(pi)
sind([0 30 45 60 90])
cosd(90)
tools.notes: The degree variants are both clearer and more exact than converting with deg2rad first. They do not accept complex input.

tools.name: cosd
tools.description: Computes the cosine of an angle given in degrees, returning exactly zero at odd multiples of 90. Use it in coordinate transformations and geodesy where angles come in degrees. It rejects complex input, unlike `cos`.
tools.example:
cosd(90)
cosd([0 60 120 180])
lat = 45;
kmPerDegLon = 111.32 * cosd(lat)
tools.notes: Pair with `sind` for rotation matrices built from degree angles.

tools.name: tand
tools.description: Computes the tangent of an angle in degrees, returning Inf exactly at odd multiples of 90 where the function has poles. Use it for slopes and grades expressed in degrees. As with the other degree variants, complex input is not supported.
tools.example:
tand(45)
tand(90)
gradePercent = 100 * tand(5)
tools.notes: tand(90) is Inf while tan(pi/2) is a large finite number, another reason to prefer the degree variants when your data is in degrees.

tools.name: sinh
tools.description: Computes the hyperbolic sine, (e^x - e^-x)/2, elementwise. Hyperbolic functions appear in catenary curves, transmission line equations, relativistic rapidity and some activation functions. The inverse is `asinh`.
tools.example:
sinh(0)
sinh(1)
x = linspace(-3, 3, 7);
[sinh(x); cosh(x)]
tools.notes: sinh overflows to Inf for arguments above about 710. `asinh` is well conditioned everywhere, unlike `acosh` and `atanh` which have restricted real domains.

tools.name: cosh
tools.description: Computes the hyperbolic cosine, (e^x + e^-x)/2, which is always at least 1 for real input. It describes the shape of a hanging cable (catenary) and appears throughout wave and heat equations. The inverse `acosh` requires input of at least 1 for real results.
tools.notes: cosh overflows above about 710 like sinh. For numerical stability in log-domain computations use `log(cosh(x))` carefully or the identity abs(x) + log1p(exp(-2*abs(x))) - log(2).

tools.name: tanh
tools.description: Computes the hyperbolic tangent, a smooth sigmoid saturating at -1 and +1. It is widely used as a squashing nonlinearity in neural networks and control laws, and as a soft clipping function in audio processing. The inverse `atanh` is defined on (-1, 1).
tools.notes: tanh saturates numerically to exactly 1 for arguments above about 20, so gradients vanish in that region. It never overflows, unlike sinh and cosh.

tools.name: atanh
tools.description: Computes the inverse hyperbolic tangent, defined on (-1, 1) for real results and complex elsewhere. It is the Fisher z-transform used to stabilize the variance of correlation coefficients, and appears in information theory and in the logit family. The related inverses are `asinh` and `acosh`.

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Numeric array; real values must lie in (-1,1) for real output.

tools.example:
atanh(0.5)
r = 0.8;
z = atanh(r)          % Fisher transform
r2 = tanh(z)
atanh(1)
tools.notes: atanh(1) is Inf and atanh(-1) is -Inf. Values with magnitude above 1 return complex results.

tools.name: deg2rad
tools.description: Converts angles from degrees to radians by multiplying by pi/180. Use it at the boundary where degree-valued data enters radian-based math, keeping the conversion explicit and readable. `rad2deg` performs the inverse conversion.
tools.example:
deg2rad(180)
deg2rad([0 90 270])
sin(deg2rad(30))
sind(30)
tools.notes: When all your math can stay in degrees, the `sind`/`cosd` family avoids the conversion entirely and is exact at the cardinal angles.

tools.name: rad2deg
tools.description: Converts angles from radians to degrees by multiplying by 180/pi. Use it when presenting computed angles to users or writing them to files that expect degrees. It is the inverse of `deg2rad`.
tools.notes: Combine with `mod(x, 360)` to keep headings in the conventional 0 to 360 range.

tools.name: unwrap
tools.description: Removes 2*pi discontinuities from a phase vector by adding or subtracting multiples of 2*pi whenever consecutive samples jump by more than a tolerance. Use it after `angle` or `atan2` to obtain a continuous phase curve for phase-response plots and group-delay computations. The jump tolerance and the operating dimension are both adjustable.
tools.usage:
Q = unwrap(P)
Q = unwrap(P, tol)
Q = unwrap(P, tol, dim)
tools.notes: Unwrapping fails when the true phase changes by more than pi between samples, so sample densely. `unwrap(p, [], 2)` unwraps along rows.

tools.name: complex
tools.description: Constructs a complex array from real and imaginary parts, and crucially keeps the complex attribute even when the imaginary part is zero. Use it when a function or generated C code requires a complex-typed input regardless of the current values. Writing `a + 1i*b` instead would silently produce a real array when b is all zeros.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Imaginary part; defaults to zero but still marks the result complex.

tools.example:
z = complex(3, 4)
zz = complex([1 2], 0);
isreal(zz)
isreal(1 + 0i)
tools.notes: `isreal(complex(1,0))` is false while `isreal(1+0i)` is true, because MATLAB drops an all-zero imaginary part in ordinary arithmetic. This matters for MEX and Coder interfaces.

tools.name: real
tools.description: Returns the real part of each element of a complex array, and the value itself for real input. Use it to discard tiny imaginary residues left by numerically symmetric operations such as an inverse FFT of a conjugate-symmetric spectrum. Always check the size of the discarded imaginary part before assuming it is noise.
tools.example:
real(3 + 4i)
y = ifft(fft([1 2 3 4]));
max(abs(imag(y)))
real(y)
tools.notes: `ifft(..., 'symmetric')` avoids the need for `real` after an inverse FFT and is faster. Silently taking the real part can hide genuine bugs.

tools.name: imag
tools.description: Returns the imaginary part of each element, and zeros for real input. Use it to separate quadrature components, to inspect numerical error after operations that should produce real results, and with `real` to convert between rectangular and polar forms. The result is always a real array.
tools.example:
imag(3 + 4i)
z = exp(1i * pi/3);
[real(z) imag(z)]
[abs(z) angle(z)]
tools.notes: imag of a real array is a zero array of the same size, not an error. Pair with `real`, `abs` and `angle` for the four standard decompositions.

tools.name: conj
tools.description: Returns the complex conjugate of each element, negating the imaginary part. Use it for inner products of complex vectors, for constructing conjugate-symmetric spectra, and in the definition of power and correlation for complex signals. Real input is returned unchanged.
tools.example:
conj(3 + 4i)
z = [1+1i, 2-3i];
z * z'          % conjugate inner product
sum(z .* conj(z))
abs(z).^2
tools.notes: The `'` operator already conjugates; use `.'` when you want to transpose without conjugation. z.*conj(z) equals abs(z).^2 up to rounding.

tools.name: angle
tools.description: Returns the phase angle of each complex element in radians, in the interval (-pi, pi]. It is equivalent to atan2(imag(z), real(z)) and is the standard way to obtain the phase response of a filter or the argument of a complex number. Follow it with `unwrap` for a continuous phase curve.
tools.notes: The phase of a value whose magnitude is essentially zero is meaningless noise; mask small magnitudes before plotting phase.

tools.name: isreal
tools.description: Returns true when an array has no imaginary part stored, which is subtly different from asking whether all imaginary values are zero. Use it to branch between real and complex code paths and to validate inputs. To test that values are effectively real, compare `max(abs(imag(z)))` against a tolerance instead.
tools.example:
isreal([1 2 3])
isreal(1 + 0i)
isreal(complex(1, 0))
isreal(sqrt(-1))
tools.notes: Operations that could produce complex results, such as `sqrt` of a possibly-negative array, mark the output complex even when all imaginary parts turn out to be zero, until an operation drops them.

tools.name: gamma
tools.description: Evaluates the gamma function, the continuous extension of the factorial with gamma(n) = (n-1)! for positive integers. Use it in probability densities, combinatorial formulas with non-integer arguments and special-function identities. It has poles at zero and the negative integers, where it returns Inf.
tools.example:
gamma(5)
factorial(4)
gamma(0.5)
sqrt(pi)
gamma(0)
tools.notes: gamma overflows above about 171.6 for doubles; use `gammaln` and work in the log domain for large arguments. `gammainc` gives the incomplete gamma function.

tools.name: gammaln
tools.description: Computes the natural logarithm of the gamma function without overflowing, for arguments where gamma itself would be astronomically large. Use it for log-likelihoods of gamma, Poisson, beta and Dirichlet distributions and for log binomial coefficients. It accepts nonnegative real input.
tools.example:
gammaln(1000)
log(gamma(1000))
logNchooseK = @(n,k) gammaln(n+1) - gammaln(k+1) - gammaln(n-k+1);
exp(logNchooseK(10, 3))
tools.notes: Computing log(gamma(x)) directly returns Inf for x above about 171; gammaln stays finite to very large arguments.

tools.name: beta
tools.description: Evaluates the beta function B(z,w) = gamma(z)*gamma(w)/gamma(z+w), which normalizes the beta distribution and appears in binomial and F-distribution formulas. Use `betaln` for the logarithm when arguments are large, and `betainc` for the incomplete beta function and its associated cumulative distributions. Inputs must be nonnegative and are expanded elementwise.

parameters.name: Z, W
parameters.description: Nonnegative real arrays with compatible sizes.

tools.example:
beta(2, 3)
gamma(2)*gamma(3)/gamma(5)
betaln(500, 500)
betainc(0.5, 2, 3)
tools.notes: beta underflows to 0 for large arguments, so switch to `betaln`. `betaincinv` inverts the incomplete beta function.

tools.name: erf
tools.description: Evaluates the error function, the integral of the Gaussian density scaled to approach 1 at infinity. Use it to express normal cumulative probabilities without a statistics toolbox, and in diffusion and heat-conduction solutions. The result lies in (-1, 1) and erf(0) is exactly 0.
tools.example:
erf(0)
erf(1)
normcdf = @(x, mu, s) 0.5 * (1 + erf((x - mu) ./ (s * sqrt(2))));
normcdf(1.96, 0, 1)
tools.notes: For x above about 6, erf(x) rounds to exactly 1, so use `erfc` to retain precision in the tail. `erfcx` is the scaled complementary error function for very large arguments.

tools.name: erfc
tools.description: Evaluates the complementary error function, 1 - erf(x), computed in a way that preserves accuracy far out in the tail where the direct subtraction would lose all significant digits. Use it for tail probabilities, bit error rate calculations and Q-function evaluation. It underflows to 0 only around x = 27.
tools.example:
erfc(5)
1 - erf(5)
Q = @(x) 0.5 * erfc(x / sqrt(2));
ber = Q(sqrt(2 * 10^(7/10)))
tools.notes: Always prefer erfc to 1-erf for tail work. `erfcinv` inverts it and `erfinv` inverts erf.

tools.name: erfinv
tools.description: Computes the inverse error function, returning x such that erf(x) equals the input. Use it to convert probabilities into standard deviations, for example to compute a z-score for a given confidence level without a statistics toolbox. Input must lie in [-1, 1]; the endpoints return -Inf and Inf.
tools.example:
erfinv(0)
norminv = @(p) sqrt(2) * erfinv(2*p - 1);
norminv(0.975)
erfinv(1)
tools.notes: For probabilities very close to 0 or 1, `erfcinv` is better conditioned than erfinv.

tools.name: besselj
tools.description: Evaluates the Bessel function of the first kind J_nu(Z), the solution to Bessel's equation that is finite at the origin. These functions describe vibration modes of circular membranes, diffraction patterns, and wave propagation in cylindrical geometry. Orders and arguments are expanded elementwise.
tools.usage:
J = besselj(nu, Z)
J = besselj(nu, Z, scale)

parameters.name: nu
parameters.description: Order; may be non-integer or negative.

parameters.name: scale
parameters.description: 1 to scale the result by exp(-abs(imag(Z))) to avoid overflow.

tools.example:
besselj(0, 0)
x = linspace(0, 20, 400);
plot(x, besselj(0, x), x, besselj(1, x))
legend('J_0', 'J_1')
tools.notes: `bessely`, `besseli` and `besselk` give the second-kind, modified first-kind and modified second-kind functions. Use the scaling flag for large imaginary arguments where besseli and besselk overflow.

tools.name: bessely
tools.description: Evaluates the Bessel function of the second kind Y_nu(Z), also called the Neumann function, which is singular at the origin. Use it together with `besselj` to form the general solution of Bessel's equation in annular geometries and in scattering problems. It returns -Inf at Z = 0 for real arguments.
tools.usage:
Y = bessely(nu, Z)
Y = bessely(nu, Z, scale)
tools.example:
bessely(0, 1)
x = linspace(0.1, 20, 400);
plot(x, bessely(0, x), x, bessely(1, x))
ylim([-1 1])
tools.notes: Y functions diverge logarithmically at 0, so start plots away from the origin. Hankel functions are formed as besselj(nu,z) + 1i*bessely(nu,z).

tools.name: legendre
tools.description: Computes the associated Legendre functions of degree n and all orders m = 0..n for each element of the input. These appear in spherical harmonics, multipole expansions and geopotential models. The output has one extra leading dimension of size n+1 holding the orders.
tools.usage:
P = legendre(n, X)
P = legendre(n, X, normalization)

parameters.name: normalization
parameters.description: 'unnorm' (default), 'sch' for Schmidt semi-normalized, or 'norm' for fully normalized.

tools.example:
P = legendre(2, [0 0.5 1])
size(P)
P(1, :)    % order m = 0
legendre(3, cosd(30), 'norm')
tools.notes: Unnormalized values overflow for degrees above roughly 150; use 'norm' or 'sch' for high-degree spherical harmonic work.

tools.name: ellipke
tools.description: Computes the complete elliptic integrals of the first and second kind for parameter m, returning both K and E. They appear in pendulum periods, the arc length of an ellipse, and inductance and field calculations for circular coils. The parameter m must lie in [0, 1].
tools.usage:
K = ellipke(M)
[K, E] = ellipke(M)
[K, E] = ellipke(M, tol)
tools.example:
[K, E] = ellipke(0.5)
ellipke(0)
pi/2
theta0 = deg2rad(30);
T = 4 * sqrt(1/9.81) * ellipke(sin(theta0/2)^2)
tools.notes: MATLAB uses the parameter convention m = k^2, not the modulus k; check which convention a reference uses before comparing values. `ellipj` gives the Jacobi elliptic functions.

tools.name: factorial
tools.description: Computes n! for each nonnegative integer element, implemented as gamma(n+1). Use it for small combinatorial counts and series coefficients. Results above 21! are not exactly representable in double precision, so treat large values as approximate.
tools.example:
factorial(5)
factorial(0:4)
factorial(170)
factorial(171)
tools.notes: factorial(171) overflows to Inf. For log factorials use `gammaln(n+1)`, and for exact big-integer factorials use Symbolic Math Toolbox.

tools.name: nchoosek
tools.description: With a scalar n it returns the binomial coefficient 'n choose k'; with a vector it returns a matrix of all k-element combinations of the vector's elements. Use it for combinatorial counts and for exhaustively enumerating subsets in small search problems. The combination form grows explosively, so MATLAB warns for large inputs.
tools.usage:
b = nchoosek(n, k)
C = nchoosek(v, k)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Scalar count, or a vector whose combinations are enumerated.

tools.example:
nchoosek(10, 3)
C = nchoosek([1 2 3 4], 2)
size(C)
nchoosek("abcd", 2)
tools.notes: Results become inexact above about n = 53 for the scalar form; use `exp(gammaln(n+1)-gammaln(k+1)-gammaln(n-k+1))` or rounded logs for large n. `perms` enumerates permutations.

tools.name: primes
tools.description: Returns a row vector of all prime numbers less than or equal to a limit, computed with a sieve of Eratosthenes. Use it to build prime tables for number-theoretic work, testing and cryptographic toy examples. Memory grows with the limit, so very large limits are impractical.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Upper bound, a nonnegative integer scalar.

tools.example:
primes(30)
numel(primes(1000))
last = max(primes(100))
tools.notes: To test a single number use `isprime`, which is far cheaper than generating a full table. `factor` returns the prime factorization.

tools.name: isprime
tools.description: Tests each element for primality, returning a logical array. Use it to filter candidate values, in number-theory exercises and to validate parameters that must be prime, such as some hash table sizes. Input must consist of nonnegative integers.

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Array of nonnegative integers (double or integer class).

tools.example:
isprime([2 4 7 9 11])
v = 1:50;
v(isprime(v))
isprime(uint64(2^31 - 1))
tools.notes: Very large values beyond flintmax cannot be tested reliably in double precision; use an integer class. Symbolic Math Toolbox handles arbitrary-precision primality.

tools.name: factor
tools.description: Returns the prime factors of a positive integer as a sorted row vector, with repeated factors listed as many times as they occur. Use it for number-theory work, for finding common factors when simplifying ratios, and for exploring the structure of integers. The product of the returned vector reproduces the input.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Positive integer scalar (double or integer class).

tools.notes: factor accepts only scalars, and values above flintmax cannot be factored accurately in double precision. Combine with `unique` and `accumarray` to get exponents.
